newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE-India power generator makers see bright future.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-India power generator makers see bright future.

text.p: Shoppers in one of Delhi's most fashionable shopping areas, South Extension, grimace in the midday heat as the power supply abruptly fails, silencing the baritone hum of air-conditioners.
A few doors away, S. Rajagopalan is beaming broadly at the onset of yet another Indian power cut.

Rajagopalan is the vice-president of marketing and sales at Birla Yamaha Ltd, one of the two major Indian manufacturers of power generator sets who are rolling in cash while the country reels under an acute power shortage.
"It is a very happy situation," he says cheerfully. "Somebody's problem is somebody else's opportunity."
Rajagopalan knows what he is talking about.
After accumulating losses that ran to more than 21 million rupees ($585,000) until 1994, Birla Yamaha turned the corner in 1995/96 (April-March) by cashing in on the severe electricity deficit.
In 1996/97, the company expects to make a profit of some 100 million rupees -- well above the previous year's 60.4 million rupees, Rajagopalan says.
The firm, 40 percent-owned by India's Birla family and 26 percent by Japan's Yamaha Motor Co, controls about 40 percent of the power generator market.
A WAITING-LIST? FOR A GENERATOR?
Its rival, Shriram Honda Power Equipment Ltd, says it is struggling to cope with the demand for its generators, which has driven it to expand capacity by 50 percent this year.
"We even have a waiting list for the one kilovolt ampere (KVA) model genset," a company spokesman says happily. "Whatever we offer is quickly lapped up."
The company, a joint venture between India's Shriram Industrial Enterprises Ltd and Japan's Honda Motor Co Ltd, controls about 60 percent of the market, estimated at some 90,000 generators in 1997.
Indian-made generators produce between 0.15 KVA and 3.0 KVA of power -- enough to run fans and lights, but not air-conditioners. Large factories import more powerful generators to run their plants.
Birla Yamaha's Rajagopalan says it expects the industry to expand by up to 15 percent annually.
The Shriram Honda spokesman agrees. "The future's great," he says. "It's boom time for the sector."
A GROWTH INDUSTRY IN POWER-STARVED INDIA
If recent Indian trends in power production are any indicator, the two firms have reason to crow over the future.
Between April 1992 and March 1997, the government created the capacity to produce only 17,000 megawatts of electricity, painfully short of a targeted 38,000 megawatts.
The federal Planning Commission says about 40,000 megawatts of capacity are expected to be added between 1997 and 2002, against an earlier estimate of 57,000 megawatts.
Power cuts in the Indian capital are a daily feature, with some parts of New Delhi going without electricity for six to eight hours a day.

Business leaders repeatedly complain that the severe power shortage is reining in industrial production. India says the shortfall costs industry $2.7 billion annually and can be bridged only through $112 billion in investment over the next 10 years.
"We don't see demand and supply equalising for the next 10 years at all," the Shriram Honda spokesman says. "And demand for gensets is a function of the power deficit."

"I see this lasting at least a century because the kind of investment required for power plants is just not coming, the returns are not immediate and nobody knows what government we'll have after two years," he adds, laughing.
Both generator makers scoff at the suggestion of competition from cheaper, battery-operated inverters, which they say require more maintenance and must be recharged between power cuts.
"Inverters are sold only by the small-scale sector. There is no after-sales service and no brand in question," the Shriram Honda spokesman says.

"A customer who has bought an inverter comes to you as a confirmed customer, because he has already recognised the need for an alternative source of power and is dissatisfied with the inverter," says Rajagopalan.
BLISTERING BATTLE FOR MARKET SUPREMACY
The two companies are locked in a blistering battle for market supremacy that focuses on Indian households.
"Shops have already accepted the concept that they shouldn't make a loss due to power cuts," the Shriram Honda spokesman explained.
"But to date, we are still facing problems in trying to convince a guy to spend 20,000 rupees ($560) on a generator. He would rather buy a washing machine as a first priority."
He said the firm planned to train its eyes on southern India, where the weather is warm throughout the year.
Birla Yamaha's speciality is a range of generators that start by turning a key rather than by pulling a string, which he said the elderly and women find difficult, Rajagopalan said.
"Day by day, the customer wants more convenience," he said.
As summer set in, Shriram Honda placed advertisements in newspapers depicting an affluent, but wistful, young housewife.
"He's given you a washing machine, an oven and a refrigerator. Pity he hasn't given you the power to use them," it said.
Two days later, Birla Yamaha shot back: "He's given you a washing machine, an oven, a refrigerator. He's given you a genset. But has he given you the key to start it?"
